maintopic: STATEMENT OP SIR GEORGE PERLEY CONCERNING VISIT TO SOUTH AMERICA

speechtext:
Right Hon. Sir GEORGE PERLEY (Minister without Portfolio) moved that the house go into committee of supply.
He said: Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I think this would be a suitable time for me to say a few words about the cruise to South America in which I took part. In the first place I should like to explain how this cruise originated. A good many months ago the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, which we all know is a strong organization in this country and which has sponsored missions to other parts of the world on behalf of Canadian business, decided that it would be advisable to arrange a mission to various countries in South America, stopping at the West Indies en route. In this enterprise the Canadian Manufacturers' Association co-operated and eventually, through an arrangement with the Canadian National'Steamship Company, it was decided to use the steamship Prince Robert for the purpose of the cruise. This steamship is one of the new boats of the Canadian National Steamship Company; it was built for service on the Pacific coast, and although not large was very suitable for the purpose. It turned out to be an excellent sea boat with good accommodation.
As arrangements for this mission proceeded it became evident that a great many representative Canadians were going to take part. After giving consideration to the request of those who were organizing the mission, the government decided to send one of its number with the mission to South America for the purpose of giving it a somewhat more official backing. Naturally our colleague the Minis-

ter of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) would have been the proper person to go on the cruise, but he was unable to do so. May I express at this time the pleasure of hon. members on this side of the house, and I am sure those oh the other side, that our friend who is one of the veteran members of the house has made such a complete recovery and is again with us. As the Minister of Trade and Commerce was not able to go at the time of the cruise it fell to my lot to take his place as best I could, and therefore it was my pleasure and duty on this mission to represent the Canadian government. At the same time the mission was in no sense of an official or governmental character. However, I did what I could to assist in achieving the object of the mission and to bring its purposes before all the countries we visited.
The original object of the mission was one of trade and good will. Some people have characterized it as a cruise of merchant adventurers to the southern seas. We went with the hope of increasing business with these various countries, but the sailing of the ship was arranged so that the delegation would be at Buenos Aires at the time of the opening of the British Empire exhibition by His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales. The abject of our trip was to strengthen our friendly relations with the peoples of the various countries we visited and to endeavour to increase our business and trade with them. As I understood it my duty was to assist in every possible way to bring about that objective. When I made official visits to the President of Cuba, Uruguay, Argentina and Brazil I took some of the members of the mission with me and explained the object of our cruise; at the same time strongly urging on those presidents and other officials that they should organize return visits to this country in order that their business men might come to Canada and by meeting with us afford us the opportunity of returning the courtesies which were extended to our representatives. I also took the opportunity on behalf of the government and the people of Canada to extend to each of the presidents personally, as well as to the peoples of the countries they represented, our most friendly greetings. I am happy to say that we received a warm welcome everywhere and our greetings were reciprocated heartily by the president of the republic in which we happened to be.
May I say in passing that press men and photographers were very much in evidence in the South American countries. I have had many years experience in London, and hon. members know how many pictures are taken by photographers. I think I am safe in say-

South America-Sir George Perley
ing, however, that there were more photographs taken per day in our South American trip than I had experienced before.

maintopic: STATEMENT OP SIR GEORGE PERLEY CONCERNING VISIT TO SOUTH AMERICA
speechtext:
Undoubtedly that was due
to the good looks of the delegation.

maintopic: STATEMENT OP SIR GEORGE PERLEY CONCERNING VISIT TO SOUTH AMERICA
speechtext:
Certainly. I
appreciate the remarks of the hon. gentleman, but I regard the interest of the press men and photographers as an evidence of confidence in and friendly feeling towards Canadians as a whole. We received an enthusiastic reception wherever we went. I cannot speak too highly of the welcome we received, and when they come here-we asked our South American friends to return our visit-I am sure we shall remember how well we were treated in their country and give them a warm welcome in return.
We stopped for a day at Montevideo, the capital of Uruguay. Several of the officials of the government and the city came on board to welcome us, and they had on the wharf a very fine band, which as we disembarked played O Canada and the Maple Leaf. That afternoon the President and the Minister of Foreign Affairs received the whole party and shook hands with each one. They extended moat friendly greetings to the people of Canada. Unfortunately we were able to stay in Montevideo for only a few hours, our ship being late in reaching there on account of a severe storm. Montevideo is a delightful city, beautifully situated and well-kept, and we were very sorry not to be able to stay longer.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, our visit was so timed that we reached Buenos Aires on the day before the opening of the British Empire exhibition. We remained there for ten days -our longest stay anywhere during our trip. There again we were welcomed in most friendly manner, and a great many people were on the wharf to greet us. The city has a very good municipal band, and the mayor of the city

the intendente as they call him -who was very kind to us in many ways, sent the band to the wharf and we listened to the strains of The Maple Leaf and God Save The King.

maintopic: STATEMENT OP SIR GEORGE PERLEY CONCERNING VISIT TO SOUTH AMERICA
speechtext:
That is very good, but
what about new trade relations?

maintopic: STATEMENT OP SIR GEORGE PERLEY CONCERNING VISIT TO SOUTH AMERICA

maintopic: STATEMENT OP SIR GEORGE PERLEY CONCERNING VISIT TO SOUTH AMERICA
speechtext:
I am coming to
that if the hon. gentleman will allow me. It may be of interest to the house to know that we were met by one of the ministers of the Argentine cabinet, by a representative of the mayor, and also by Sir Herbert Gibson,
the president of the British Empire exhibition. Next day, Saturday the 14th of March, the exhibition was opened. Everything was admirably arranged, the weather was favourable, and the surroundings were all that could be desired. I may add that the band of the Cameron Highlanders, which had been specially sent out from England, gave us some bagpipe selections at the opening ceremony. The president, Sir Herbert Gibson, made a [DOT]few happy introductory remarks, and then His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, who spoke in both English and Spanish, declared the exhibition open. His Royal Highness always speaks well, but my feeling was that he excelled himself on that occasion. He was followed by the President of Argentina, a soldier, General Uriburu. I understand that these addresses were broadcast more widely than had ever been attempted before, and I hope many members heard them here in Ottawa.
I may add that after the formal opening of the exhibition I had the honour of escorting the two princes and the president through the Canadian buildings, and I am sure the house will be glad to . learn that the building and the exhibits were in every way a credit to the Dominion. For this .very satisfactory condition of affairs our exhibition commissioner, Mr. Turcotte, is to be highly commended. It was my observation that the fact of Canada taking part in a British Empire exhibition in a foreign country was a concrete example of inter-imperial co-operation, and although the Canadian building was praised by everyone, I feel that our exhibit produced a much greater impression as part of a British Empire exhibition than if Canada had been there alone. The princes and the president went through our building and expressed themselves as very much pleased with the exhibit. In this way the Prince of Wales again showed that he was representing not only Great Britain but [DOT] every part of the empire. A sergeant and three Royal Canadian Mounted Policemen were sent down to Buenos Aires to look after our building, and they created a very favourable impression. On the opening day when the princes and the president came through they were on duty and tactfully and courteously controlled the crowds that always besiege the Prince of Wales wherever he goes.
Perhaps this may be no news to hon. members, but it is worth while mentioning that by arrangements made through the telephone companies I was able to hold a conversation with the Prime Minister twice during our stay in Buenos Aires, and our thanks are due to those companies for the excellent and sat-

South America-Sir George Perley
isfactory arrangement they made. On the day of our departure I also had a talk with the Canadian High Commissioner in London and I could understand him very well indeed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, my impressions of Argentina and its people are very happy indeed. It is a fine country, the climate is delightful, and Buenos Aires, or B.A. as they call it down there, is a well-built, well-kept city, twice as large as Montreal-something that I never realized before I went there- and the people are very friendly and desirous of increasing their trade relations with us in every way possible. The Canadian mission received a hearty welcome from everyone, from the president down. The Argentine chamber of commerce made arrangements for us to see all the interesting places in the city and surrounding country, including one of their estancias, or very large ranches, which are typical of the country. Just to show that His Royal Highness was looking after Canadians as he looked after other Britishers, one morning the Prince of Wales received all the male members of our mission at the residence of the ambassador and shook hands with them and said a few words.
As I said before, I have suggested many times that this visit should be returned as soon as possible, and among other messages, I had a telegram asking me to invite delegates and visitors to attend the world's grain exhibition and conference at Regina in July, 1932. This I did, in speaking one evening at a dinner, and I am glad to have received today a circular from the world's grain exhibition at Regina saying that an official mission has been appointed by the government of Argentina to represent that country at that exhibition. I consider this very welcome news, and the fact that these people are coming from so far away certainly adds to the importance of our exhibition.
So that you may have some idea of the feeling of the people of Argentina towards Canada, Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to a speech delivered by the Minister of Agriculture and Commerce on the day we left Buenos Aires. I gave a luncheon that day to all the men of our mission and to prominent residents of Buenos Aires. They favoured me with about two hundred guests, including three members of the Argentine government, the British ambassador and the president of the British Empire exhibition. I proposed the toast to our guests on that occasion, which was seconded by my friend Colonel Woods of Calgary, and after the British ambassador said a few words in reply, the Argentine Minister of Agriculture and Commerce spoke in Spanish. He was good enough

to send me a translated copy of his address, of which I should like to read a portion:
There are events of which actors are seldom fit to appreciate the importance of and consequences; but on this occasion the visit of the Canadian mission is of such importance that it is not possible to hide the consequences involved.
Our countries, being placed opposite one another on the American continent, reaching both the inhabited zones nearing the extreme poles, it seems as if the long distance separating them would be a great hindrance to their comprehension, but the mission presided over by such an eminent personality as our host and the qualified character of our visitors, is the most striking evidence of our resemblance in many moral and material respects which closely bind us in mutual links.
The race so vigorously arisen in Canada, having the fundamental pith of the French pioneers, followed by the magnificent effort of the Britons, who further enhance the progressive striving, convey to us grace, merriment, intelligence and truthfulness, in such a manner that we heartily seek to call you our great friends the Canadians.
Then we left Buenos Aires, and on our way back we stopped at Rio de Janeiro. Ever since I was a boy I have heard about the beauty of the city and harbour of Rio, but I must say the reality surpassed all my expectations. The city is built on the sides of hills and in the valleys between; there is a wonderful land-locked bay twenty-five miles or more in length, which can very well claim to be one of the most beautiful harbours in the world. There we received another warm welcome. The Brazilian government were gracious enough to send a representative from the foreign office to the ship, and they made my wife and myself and Right Hon. Chief Justice Anglin and Mrs. Anglin the guests of the nation on that occasion. I never had a more friendly reception than I received when we called on the Foreign Secretary. The government, together with the Rio de Janeiro chamber of commerce gave us a luncheon, at which the Minister of Commerce and Labour occupied the chair. He proposed our health in English, and in order to show the feeling in Brazil with regard to Canada I am going to take the liberty of reading a portion of his speech on that occasion:
Members of the Canadian mission, your visit is particularly agreeable to us. We know that alongside of outstanding figures in politics, there are with us at this moment the most representative persons in Canadian finance, commerce and industry. We feel certain that Brazil cannot but gain by being known, if only by means of such a rapid visit, by a group of such distinguished men, men of intelligence and action.
If it be true that the international politics of our days more and more tend to economic factors, and become increasingly subordinate to

South America-Sir George Perley
determinations in inter-commerce, it should be beyond doubt that infinite are the possibilities open for attachments between Canada and Brazil, geographically, two of the largest expressions of the New World, of completely diverse climate and production, and whose interests do not collide, but which really complement one another in all phases of world competition.
Commercial relations between Canada and Brazil are only in their beginning, the result so far only of private initiative. We can be, and w'e already are being, an excellent market for the placing of various manufactured products of your country. You have, besides this, wheat to bring to Brazil. In exchange we are in a position to furnish you with many products and raw materials essential to your economy. More than half the coffee which you consume is not yet supplied by Brazil. We have here, right now, a magnificent field for reciprocal benefits, capable of increasing the volume of our tra*le. Canadian rubber products already enjoy an excellent position in Brazilian markets. The facility which you could offer for the importation of our "Caoutchouc" appears of intuitive convenience and large are your possibilities to supply the consuming markets of Brazil with Canadian manufactured products.
The day before we left Rio de Janeiro we were all invited to pay the president a visit at his summer home at Petropolis, which is about forty-five miles from Rio and 2,500 feet above sea level. There the president and his wife received all the members of our mission and sent most friendly greetings to the government and the people of Canada.
On	the way	down we made	a visit atTrinidad, and on the way back we stopped at Bermuda. They, like ourselves, form part of the British Empire, and needless to say they	received	us with open arms.	I wassorry	that we	were unable to	visit	otherBritish islands, but I may say that the sentiment in Trinidad and Bermuda is strongly favourable to Canada. They appreciate the fine service given them by the Canadian National steamships and the advantages which have	accrued	to them through	the	trade
agreement entered into a few years ago. While I was there I was told that the West Indies and Bermuda were thinking of sending a trade commissioner to Canada to represent those islands. It seems to me this would be a very wise thing, and I hope it will be done in the near future.
In regard to the business ipart of this mission, as I said before, this was under the auspices of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, of which Colonel J. H. Woods, of Calgary, is president, and of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the president of which is Mr. Elmer Davis. They had a very efficient secretary in the person of Mr. Wendell Clarke. Wherever we stopped the representatives of the chambers of commerce, of the merchants
and of the boards of trade came on board to welcome our mission, and in nearly every instance escorted the mission to a meeting specially convened for the purpose.
On the way south the mission held a meeting at which committees were appointed to make reports on various aspects of trade and business relations as they presented themselves on the trip. They gave a great deal of consideration to this matter, and on the way back, at a special meeting, they put in their reports, which were then referred to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. The reports have been sent out in printed form, along with an excellent condensed report signed by these two presidents, Colonel Woods and Mr. Davis.
I am not in any way responsible for these reports, and they are in no sense official. At the same time, however, they have been considered and approved by these two strong organizations, and they contain a good deal of useful information and many wise suggestions. I believe that members of the 'house have all received copies of the report made by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce with respect to the mission. I shall read a part of the general report, and if any hon. members are not in possession of copies I shall be glad to lay two or three of them on the table, so that they may study their contents. I quote the following:
The delegation is convinced that both from the point of view of good will and practical business the mission, which it is believed is the most important one of its kind ever leaving the Dominion, has been a very outstanding success. The people of Cuba, Uruguay, of the Argentine, of Brazil, of Trinidad and Bermuda, gave ample evidence of their desire and even eagerness to increase their commercial relations with the Dominion of Canada. This desire was particularly manifest in the Argentine and was prompted, not only by the visit of the mission itself, but also by the very excellent exhibits of the products of the Dominion, displayed in the Canadian pavilion at the British Empire trade fair at Buenos Aires.
The delegation was impressed with the very great hospitality and kindness of the peoples of the countries visited. The members of the party met the nationals in the different countries, for the most part as strangers, and said au revoir as friends. From presidents, ministers of state, governors, mayors, presidents of chambers of commerce and the business community generally, the mission received the most cordial of receptions and was welcomed in a fashion which left no doubt as to tbe depth and extent of the kindness and friendliness offered the Canadians.
The delegation are of the opinion that out of the total import trade of Latin America, amounting to about two and a half billion dollars a year, Canada's contribution of thirty-

South America-Sir George Perley
nine million dollars can be substantially increased and that out of the three billion dollars which are exported from Latin America, Canada's purchases of some twenty-nine million can be profitably expanded.
The mission are further of the opinion that in the developing of Canada's trade with Latin America, emphasis should be laid, not only on our exports thereto, but also on our purchases therefrom. Even though some of the products of the Argentine, for instance, are in competition with those of Canada, much could be done to improve our present commercial situation with these countries by deflecting some.of the trade direct to Canada on Canadian steamship lines, which now passes through American ports.
The mission have noted with gratification that already some fifteen definite agencies or representations have been established as a result of its visit.
The delegation cannot speak too highly of the splendid work which is being done for Canada by the Canadian banks established in the various countries to which the mission went. These great banking institutions of Canada are proving themselves veritable spearheads for Canadian commerce.
The delegation would also recognize the contribution which the trade commissioner service is making to the promotion of Canadian export trade.
The delegation are of the opinion that a knowledge of Spanish in particular should be more widely acquired by young men in our universities and export companies, and would therefore urge upon the educational authorities of the Dominion the desirability of emphasizing this study in their curricula. Just as Canadians prefer to do business in English, so the Argentines prefer to conduct correspondence and interviews in Spanish, and the Brazilians in Portuguese.
' The desirability of Canadian producers combining and standardizing for export was clear to the mission, when such exporters, as individual companies, are not themselves in a position to establish on a satisfactory basis a strong selling and advertising organization in the Latin American countries.
The mission have noted with considerable interest that the British West Indies and Bermuda are giving immediate attention to the appointment of a trade commissioner to Canada, whose appointment is being hastened by the visit of the mission itself.
The mission was interested in noting that the government of the Argentine has approved in principle the plan to build during the next three years nine hundred grain elevators at six hundred points, the program to involve an expenditure of some twenty million dollars during the next three years, and that Canadian contractors are making a bid for this business.
The agricultural committee of the mission see many advantages to be gained by an exchange of breeding stock and cattle judges between the Argentine and Canada, and recommend that steps be taken immediately to bring about this desired objective. The agricultural committee further point out the demand in the Argentine for the better quality silver fox fur pelts of Canada; the opening for Canadian live poultry in the Argentine and Brazil; and the market in Trinidad for bee supplies from Canada. It may be noted that Trinidad pro-
[Sir George PerleyJ
poses to exhibit its agricultural products at the Canadian National exhibition this year.
The foregoing, as I have said, is from the report of the mission. Now, I think I am safe in saying that we accomplished the object of our mission. We established friendly relations and got into personal touch not only with prominent people in these South American countries, but with the governments themselves.
We all realize how helpful it is to know people personally, and how much easier it is then to do business with them. It is true we found them all prepared to welcome the mission most heartily, as evidently they had already formed a good opinion of Canada. However, our trip enabled the mission and its members to get into personal conta*t with the officials and business men of the countries we visited, and I feel strongly that our manufacturers and merchants should be able to increase their business in South America by taking prompt advantage of the impression that has been created there by the mission.
Several of the members obtained orders and made contacts in the Various places visited, and this should certainly be followed up not only by them but also by other business firms in Canada. We must always bear in mind, however-I cannot emphasize this too strongly-that there is keen competition for the South American market, and to obtain the best results the principals should go down there rather than send representatives. They should go themselves for the purpose of meeting these people personally, and I am sure that business would be much more likely to result from that course.
Our trade commissioners w'ill be found helpful in every way, and it is a fact that the Canadian banks and insurance and light companies have. by their business capacity and fair dealing created an atmosphere favourable to all Canadians. We had on this trip 150 Canadians. All on board were Canadians with the exception of our friend Mr. Pratt, who is president of the Newfoundland board of trade. We were happy to have him with us, and vee got along as though we were all from the same country. This led me to hope that some day or other the desirable result might be brought about, of Newfoundland and Canada becoming one, as it seems to me they really ought to be.
These Canadians on board were a very representative lot: they were of both French and English extraction and they created a good impression wherever they went. We travelled for six or seven weeks on this ship and we got along very well together, and I believe the whole party came back to Halifax

South America-Mr. Mackenzie King
feeling that they had had a most interesting and useful trip. May I here express most grateful thanks to Colonel Woods, Mr. Davis, and Mr. Robb, the vice-president of the Canadian National Railways, and all the other members of the mission for their unfailing kindness and courtesy throughout the entire trip to Lady Perley and myself.
I was particularly impressed with three things during this mission. In the first place,
I cannot speak strongly enough of the wonderful welcome received everywhere. The people of South America are very friendly to Canada and desire closer relations with us, and when they make a return visit, which I hope will be very soon, we must and will give them a very hearty welcome. Then it was brought home to me quite forcibly, that the British Empire should keep together as a commercial entity as well as from sentiment, and there is no doubt that the favourable impression created in the Argentine was increased by the fact that Canada was there at this exhibition alongside the mother country. Everyone felt that our building and exhibit was a marked success, but I do not think it would have been as successful if it had not been part of the British Empire exhibition. I was impressed also with the fact that we Canadians can do almost anything when we work well together. On this voyage we had representatives from all parts of this country, every race and every political party was represented, but no question of party affiliation or birth or creed was ever discussed. We pulled together and we accomplished what we went for and I believe we created a most satisfactory and favourable impression in South America.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: STATEMENT OP SIR GEORGE PERLEY CONCERNING VISIT TO SOUTH AMERICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that the remarks of the right hon. minister (Sir George Perley) call for any acknowledgment from this side of the house, but inasmuch as he has given such an interesting account of the mission on which he was the representative of the government, I may be permitted to say a word.
As the minister has mentioned, the trip to South America and the West Indies was in the nature of an unofficial mission. It was not a government mission. As, however, the government considered desirable the appointment of a representative thereon, it is fitting that this House of Commons should have from him some account of the journey, and its significant events and results. It is proper also that fitting acknowledgment should be made of the many courtesies extended to the mission by the different countries visited, and all hon. members will appreciate the
words by which the right hon. minister has expressed on behalf of Canada his appreciation of the courtesies extended to those who accompanied him on this trip.
While we are dealing in pleasantries, may I say that this is the first opportunity I have had since my hon. friend returned, to extend to him from this side of the house congratulations upon his having been made an imperial privy councillor in recognition of his many years of public service to Canada and service to other parts of the British Empire as well. He is one of the oldest and most respected members of this house, and we on this side join very heartily with his friends opposite in congratulating him upon this high recognition of long and useful public service. We trust he may be spared many years to continue to enjoy that distinguished honour.
In listening to my right hon. friend, I was hoping that during the course of his remarks, he would indicate to us whether or not he had been able, as the representative of the government, to indicate to the various countries visited wherein the policies of the government of which he is a member might serve to encourage or facilitate trade between those countries and Canada, but I did not hear any reference to the trade policies of hon. gentlemen opposite. He did refer to the address by which His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales opened the British Empire Exhibition at Buenos Aires, and his mention of that speech with my recollection of it, caused me to send for a paper which contained the cabled account. I think I might read to my right hon. friend a paragraph from that address. It is contained in a Canadian Press despatch dated Buenos Aires, March 14, which appears in the papers of March 16, and reads as follows:
"Failure to recognize trade as interchange; obstacles placed in the way of reciprocal trade, are perhaps the main causes of the world's present troubles," declared His Royal Highness the Prince of AYales in his speech formally inaugurating the great British Empire trade exhibition here to-day.
That in a word was the burden of the thought contained in the very excellent address made by His Royal Highness in opening the exhibition. As I remember the address, it expressed from beginning to close a desire on the part of His Royal Highness that all nations should create an atmosphere of good will which would foster the interchange of goods between each other, and that the more there was in the way of interchange of commodities between nations the more quickly would the world's great problems of unemployment and the like be relieved. His Royal Highness went on to say that the atmosphere
1498	COMMONS
South America-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
of good will which brought about an interchange of commodities, and which my right hon. friend has recognized as being so important, was best created by removing many of the obstacles to trade. The most significant and important of all such obstacles to trade are tariff barriers.
My right hon. friend represents an administration with a trade policy so-called "Canada First," by which is meant that nothing is to be admitted into this country from another country which can be manufactured or produced in Canada, if a tariff barrier can be placed sufficiently high to keep it out. If that is to remain the policy of the present administration, it might as well save its money when it comes to sending missions abroad, because a policy of that kind is diametrically opposed to that saner policy which the right hon. gentleman has alluded to so approvingly as having been enunciated by His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales. I commend to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) the reading of the opening address of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales at the British Empire Exhibition, and the application, as between the different nations with whom he hopes this country may do business in the future, of the policy therein laid down.

speechtext: Is that why Great Britain is so prosperous just now?

maintopic: STATEMENT OP SIR GEORGE PERLEY CONCERNING VISIT TO SOUTH AMERICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I at least can speak for myself in congratulating the right hon. gentleman (Sir George Perley) on the excellent description he has given of the very pleasant social time the mission had in South America. He seems to have, remembered every band which greeted them on every wharf, and even the tunes played. It would be unfair on my part to criticize the mission because it did not offer to this country any hope of the development of trade relations outside of the fact that more friendly social relations have been established. However, I did notice in one of the documents from w'hich the right hon. gentleman has quoted, that there was a proposal made to improve the trade between the Argentine and this country by the shipment of more manufactured goods to the Argentine while we were to take in return therefor-what would you imagine? Beef, hides, and casings, for the making, I presume, of sausages. That is the sort of thing that was suggested should be done in this publication from which the right hon. gentleman quoted. H I remember the last election correctly, and the campaign speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite, they contended that we were importing far too 
much of these commodities now, and that we should cut down our importations. If the net result of a mission of this kind is to be that we are still further to increase our importations of animal products, importations which were protested against by the present administration during the last election, then I fall to see the value in the mission. However, I take it that this mission will have better effects than that.
In regard to the address just delivered to the house by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), may I submit that, while his remarks were very pertinent, they might more properly have come from this corner than from himself. May I suggest that if it be so desirable to improve trade relations on a basis of reciprocal trade agreements, then it is too bad that greater steps in that direction were not taken during the last nine years. I am sure that my right hon. friend the present leader of the opposition must have known that he was always certain of the support of this corner of the house in any effort that he ever made or might have made to improve trade relations with other countries.

speechtext: What about butter?

maintopic: STATEMENT OP SIR GEORGE PERLEY CONCERNING VISIT TO SOUTH AMERICA
speechtext:
Yes, as regards butter, too, and anything else you like. I am afraid that my hon. friend will find that before this house gets through the butter will have turned a little rancid.
I do not think there is in this house a more courteous or more kindly man than the right hon. gentleman who has just delivered this travelogue to us (Sir George Perley). He is one of the pleasantest personalities in the house, and the house may well accept from him his representations in regard to the friendly relations that exist; but let us hope that he has come back imbued with the spirit of the words just quoted by the leader of the opposition, the words that came from the mouth of the Prince of Wales at the opening of that exhibition, and that the efforts of his administration, modified by his now maturer advice, will be in the direction of the abolition of trade barriers rather than in that of their continuation.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Tummon in the chair.
The Copper Bounties Act, 1923, administration of, $1,000.

What is
the reason for the increase of 8500 in this item?

Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
This item of $1,000 is to
pay the salaries and expenses of two inspectors. Usually, in both cases, it is an official of the customs or excise branch. Their salaries and expenses amount to three or four hundred dollars each to make an inspection of the two plants which are producing the copper upon which the bounty is paid under the Copper Bounties Act of 1923.

Item agreed to.
The Hemp Bounties Act, 1923, administration of, $500.
What is the explanation of this item?

The same explanation
virtually as I gave with regard to the previous item.
Are there any bounties being paid under this act?

Only a comparatively
small amount. The amount paid in 1930 was $3,483.
Where is this hemp grown?

A certain amount in
Manitoba and some in Ontario.

Has the minister given
any consideration to giving a bounty on wheat?

We will take that into
our consideration.

What is the quantity of
hemp raised in Canada?
I have not that information here. It is raised in scattered and comparatively small quantities. The idea of the bounty under this act was to encourage its production.

Item agreed to.
An act to place Canadian coal used in the manufacture of iron or steel on a basis of equality with imported coal, administration of, $1,000.
What is the explanation of this item?

This is to pay the salary
of a supervisor of payments in connection with the administration of this act.
Is that the act of 1930?
Yes.
What is the total amount paid out under the act in the attempt to equalize the competition?

The total amount paid
out in 1930-31 was S135,209.
How was that amount distributed by provinces?

It went to one province,
Nova Scotia, and to one company.

Upon what basis were the
payments made?

When did this act come
into force?

I cannot say just when
it came into force, but it was assented to on May 30, 1930.

The intention of this act
was to place the Nova Scotia steel works on a parity with the steel works in upper Canada, which use bituminous coal imported from the United States, upon which they got a drawback. During the election I understand that the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, brought this matter up at a meeting at Sydney, and if he did not give a direct promise, at least he left the impression that something further would be done to assist the miners in the Nova Scotia coal industry. Perhaps it might not be amiss to ask whether or not it is the intention of the government to go further in assisting the coal industry in the province of Nova Scotia?

At the moment I cannot give my hon. friend a direct answer. When the budget is brought down certain matters will be disclosed which will coyer the policy of the government with regard to the coal mining industry. At this time it would not be proper for me even to intimate the nature of -that policy.

I can readily understand
the position taken by the minister. I know that perhaps it is not the duty of the minister to give a definite answer but it is rather unfair that vce should be asked to deal with this item at the present time and to pass it without knowing something more about it. May I suggest that the item should be allowed to stand until such time as we learn the policy of the government concerning the coal industry of Nova Scotia.

I have no objection to
that. It is a very small item but there is no objection if the hon. member wishes it to stand.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

It is not the smallness of
the item which attracts my attention. There is a greater principle at stake than the mere voting of a salary, and I would suggest that the matter stand for the present.
Item stands.
British and foreign news service, $32,000.
To whom is this sum paid, and does the. government think it will receive value for the expenditure?

The item is paid and has been paid for a great many years to Reuters. I think Reuters' service is recognized by all as a very excellent international news service. There is a definite arrangement in connection with this service which I shall read if it is the desire of the committee:
The contractors agree to transmit from Canada by cable for distribution in the United Kingdom an average of 10,000 words monthly; and in addition to maintain its present cable service; to furnish the service of mail news calculated to maintain interest in Canada and Canadian activities, such news to be distributed by mail in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, South America, West Indies and India. For the purpose of carrying out these services the company will maintain in Canada a special representative who will devote his whole time to the preparation and editing of special articles, interviews, etc.
This is a useful and valuable service to Canada. I presume there might be some criticism as to whether or not the amount is too large or too small. Generally speaking however it is considered that the service has been good. The list of trade and financial publications in Great Britain regularly receiving Reuters special trade items from Canada comprises nearly two sheets of foolscap containing about 75 names of publications in Great Britain alone. The extent of these publications would give an idea of the service in Great Britain, in addition to the services rendered in other countries. I have carefully investigated the matter, and my judgment is that the service is worth while and that Canada receives value for the services rendered by Reuters under the present item.

Is Reuters a Canadian
company, and if not is there not a Canadian company which could render the same service ?

With some hesitancy I
would answer that I doubt whether there is a Canadian company equipped like Reuters to handle a similar service. The point is not that Canadians are not able to perform the task, but that the service of this great

news corporation has grown for many years. It is world wide in character, and it would take a Canadian company a great many years to build a reputation equal to that enjoyed by Reuter. Therefore I would say that at the moment under these circumstances there is no Canadian concern which could give the service rendered by Reuters.

How many agencies have
they in Canada?

I think my hon. friend
will know from his experience that the method followed is this: Reuters maintain a head office in Ottawa, and have news agents or sources of news in every city throughout the country. I suppose they have agents in all centres of consequence so far as population or activity is concerned.

I am quite sure that the
service is maintained only in the larger cities.

They have what I presume they call correspondents. For instance, newspaper men working in our cities on the staffs of the larger dailies or weekly papers, and the men in some smaller communities would receive a small fee for news supplied, according to the size and importance of the district represented. It is my understanding that they would receive a fee for acting as :orrespondents in the Reuters service.

Have they any relation
whatever with the Canadian Press service?

I cannot answer that, in
so far as their personal corporate relation with the Canadian Press is concerned.
I refer to business relations?
I understand the relations between the two services are most cordial.

There is cooperation and
cordial relationship.
Is the whole amount paid to the same company?
Yes.

Does the government exercise supervision over the character of the matter sent out by Reuters? I do not refer to censorship. I remember attacking this item when the late Mr. Robb was Minister of Finance. When the item was attacked he moved to strike out the vote, but by some means or other, at a later stage in the session he moved to reinsert it, and accordingly the vote was reinserted. The ground I took at that time was that Reuters were sending out propaganda. I would like to know if this government


Supply-Trade and Commerce
They will send out different propaganda now.
I would like to know if the government exercises any supervision over the matter sent out by Reuters?
I can assure my hon. friend that whatever might have happened in the past, no such propaganda would be sent out now.
Oh, oh.

We believe that the service is a good one. I might explain to my hon. friend that during the regime of the late Mr. Robb the item was reinstated because there was a contract with the company. For technical reasons reinstatement was made. While the government does not pretend to edit the despatches, yet through the officials of the department we keep in touch with the matter sent out, and there is a sort of general oversight. The work has been carried on to the satisfaction of the department. The service is much wider than that provided by this vote. The vote represents merely a subsidy.
Is it done under contract?

I have before me a statement- showing the work done by this organization from the years 1923 to 1931. This statement shows the number of items sent out which have been clipped from the press by our own service and despatched to the different departments affected. I will read only the totals so as to give an idea of the service rendered: In the years 1923 and 1924 there were, in round figures, 4,000; in the next year there were 12,000; in the next year 9,300; the next year, 14,000; in the next year, 13,500; in the next year, 10,000. In the two following years there were 10,000, and in the following year, 9,500. These figures show roughly the services rendered. Some despatches were short some were long, according to the importance of the items.

What are
the terms of the contract with Reuters, and over what period does it extend?
I have here a synopsis of the contract.

I just
want to know the facts.
The service rendered runs about 200,000 words during the year.

Under the contract, Reuters
specially bind themselves as to the measure of the services to be given?
*42110-96

Yes, the contract calls for
10,000	words of cable news monthly, but the actual service much exceeds that limit.

Is that news service
confined to the countries of the British Empire?
The contract specifies the British Empire, but the news frequently goes to other countries.

Must the news be of a
character to promote business, or does it cover whatever happens in this country?
All of the news is calculated to benefit inter-empire relations in the way of trade.

Some is of very doubtful
value in that connection.

Did the service include a
synopsis of the Prime Minister's speeches during the last election?
No, I do not think they were sent.

A few years ago there
was another news service included in this vote, and it had been carried on for fifteen years to my own personal knowledge, but a couple of years ago, owing to attacks made on it in this house, it was abandoned. I think it is pretty near time to abandon this one also.
Make a motion.

You people on the other side have supported this vote for so long that you have got tied up to the situation and consequently you are sitting tight. I have taken the same stand before on this item; I believe that it should be abandoned, and I am not afraid to say so now. I am not going to move any motion; it is up to you people opposite, if you want a motion, to move one. I am not afraid to attack the item, because I think it should be abandoned just for the same reason that the Associated Press service was abandoned. I do not believe that it is good business to continue this vote. If it is a matter of news, I think the people who want the news should pay for it and not the country.

Mr. Chairman, I take issue with the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Chaplin). I think this is a very valuable service. If he would pay a little closer attention to the news that is sent from Canada throughout the empire, I am inclined to think he would consider the money was well spent. When the attack was



Supply-Trade and Commerce
made on the vote before Mr. Robb offered to withdraw it, but when we made investigations we found that we would suffer very considerably in trade and otherwise if the news service was abandoned. So far as I am concerned I am prepared to support the vote.

The question I was about to ask has been largely answered, but I would suggest that the minister, being comparatively new to his office, might look very carefully into the character of the news supplied, and ascertain that the news thus subsidized-because it is subsidized-gives an absolutely impartial and accurate view of the country as a whole, and does not reflect the departmental or governmental view of things as they would wish them to be. This is rather an important matter, but in view of the assurance of the minister that the only control the government exercises is to see that unbiased news is furnished, I have no objection to the vote; but I do have very strong objection to any form of subsidized news service which may convey a picture not of conditions and opportunities actually existing, but so coloured as to give any impression which the government may wish created in the minds of those who read such news. As a matter of fact we have received too much news that gave an absolutely inaccurate picture of actual conditions and opportunities in Canada for intending immigrants. I hope that the supervision exercised by the minister will be such that the news service furnished under this vote will give an accurate picture of Canadian conditions and events.

It is all very well to have governmental control, but I think there should be some way by which the house could be informed of the character and the nature of the news sent out; for instance, a statement might very well be laid on the table of the house; then members would be in a better position to grasp what is being done.

When my hon. friend rose I was about to suggest that we would lay on the table half a ton, if you like, of these clippings covering a certain period, and members could themselves look over them. May I add this-and it is prompted by the remark of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman)-that while we were in London at the Imperial conference last autumn I had an opportunity every day of seeing the items of news supplied by Reuters. These news items were supplied officially to the trade commissioner's office in London day by day; they were not specially designed for us. I found them exceedingly valuable and useful 
in giving me a picture of Canadian trade conditions. I am not speaking now of social news or anything of that character whatever. The news items had to do purely with financial and trade affairs, and they gave me as fine a picture of the Canadian situation as I ever have received at any time from any source. I would hesitate to agree that this service has not been well-handled. The official in charge at Ottawa, Mr. Grange, is a press correspondent of very wide knowledge and experience, with whom most of the members of the house are acquainted, and we are satisfied that the work has been properly carried out. May I also add that the department has the opportunity of examining these items, and throughout the years I question if there are any to which any serious exception could be taken.
When does the contract end?

The contract with Reuters is dated June 28, 1923. It was authorized by order in council of July 27, 1923, P.C. 1391. The service was for three years, terminating July 31, 1926. The contract was extended twice, the first time by order in council of July 28, 1926, P.C., 1181, and later by order in council of October, 1926, P.C. 1583. The latter extension was from October, 1926, to the end of the fiscal year. Then a new contract was entered into in 1927 for a three year period, and another contract has been entered into for a three year period from April, 1930, so it runs until April, 1933.

In view of that statement,
while perhaps the discussion is all right to show some disapproval of the continuation of the contract, if we are to operate under the principle of the infallible justice of the crown laid down by the right hon. Prime Minister, how can we possibly cut down this amount?
We cannot do it; hon. members opposite have tied us up for three years more.
No, I think the hon. member is wrong. What was the date of the last renewal?
April, 1930.

Then the government of
that day must have thought it was proper. They must have looked into the matter carefully, and I do not think the hon. member for York-Sunbury would want the present government to repudiate a contract made under the old government, no matter how extreme he may be in his political views. I

Supply-Trade and Commerce
am sure he is fair enough to admit that the contract having been assented to for three years more, the Minister of Trade and Commerce must have looked into the matter, and he has stated to this committee that he thinks it is a right and proper contract and that the service is good. I do not think it is possible to reduce the amount, although I should like to move that-the amount be cut to $1 in order to give the hon. member for Lincoln a chance to vote against his own party and show his independence.

The hon. gentleman is
very keen to have somebody else make a motion. Now he proposes to make a motion in order to give me a chance to vote. Let me tell him that this contract was made in April, 1930, while this house was in session. Why did not the then government give us a chance to speak about it in the house, without passing an order in council?
I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if the contract was not renewed in July, 1926?
The contract was read just now by the minister; it was renewed in April, 1930.
But I understood there was a contract renewed in July, 1926.
It was extended for two months in July, 1926.
Who was the Minister of Trade and Commerce at that time?
I was not.
I should like an answer, please; who was the Minister of Trade and Commerce then?

The Minister of Trade and Commerce was the hon. member for Lincoln, I think, and I want to say that he was undoubtedly a very efficient minister. The contract was extended at that time for two months.

I should like to ask, since the hon. member for Lincoln and I have crossed swords on this matter, why at that time he did not condemn it and why he renewed it by order in council. Why did he not give us an opportunity to fight it, since we were then in apposition? It is all very well for the hon. member for Lincoln now to say that we should have brought the matter up in the house, but he did not give us an opportunity to say anything about it. I can hardly find an expression to describe the attitude of the hon. gentleman at that time.
Here he comes in and condemns the former government for having renewed the contract under order in council, when the first contract was made by his party years before. When the shadow government came in and he was the shadow Minister of Trade and Commerce, by order in council he renewed the contract. To-day he gets up and opposes the very work which he initiated or renewed at that time, and he is trying to throw the burden over on to us. This contract was initiated by the Conservative government.

The hon. gentleman is not quite right. This contract was never initiated by a Conservative government; it was initiated by the present right hon. leader of the opposition in 1923. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that there is quite a difference between renewing a contract for two months, a contract which had been in existence previously, and renewing it for a longer period when the house is in session. The hon. member for Lincoln, in the middle of an election, renewed an existing contract for a short time, to show that the matter was under consideration. He did take it under consideration. The Liberal government renewed this contract for three years at a time when this house was in session, and parliament was never consulted for a moment about it. That is the difference between the two positions.

Mr. Chairman, there is
one thing sure; if in 1926, as has been stated, I renewed the contract, I did it for two months and the reason was plain enough. I was then just as much opposed to it as I am to-day, and I would not extend the contract beyond the possible life of the government. Had I been back in that office later on, the contract never would have been continued. I did the proper thing; I only made the extension for two months instead of for three years, as the late minister did.

There is not very much use in debating the question now if the contract has no clause providing for cancellation. I should like to ask the minister if there is any provision for cancellation. Before he answers that, I should like to say that I have very grave doubts as to the efficacy of the work which is done by Reuters. I question very much whether we get $32,000 worth of work out of the service. I may say to my hon. friend the minister that my experience of the value of the service rendered does not quite coincide with his idea. I had the opportunity of being in London not quite two years ago, and I also had rendered to me the type-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
written service from Reuters' agency. It seemed to me a very meagre service indeed. It had some news, but none of very great importance, and while I say this with some hesitation, it seemed to me that very often the news was old and of no very great use to anyone. If the contract could be cancelled and anyone would make the motion, I would support it. In fact I would not hesitate very long to make the motion myself. I would move that it be cancelled, or the amount reduced to SI. I do not see much value an it.

I have not the contract
here, but the memorandum I have before me indicates that it is a three-year contract, whether or not it has the usual provision for cancellation I am not able to say definitely.

I should like to find
out from the Minister of Trade and Commerce when, after July 28, 1926, the contract was renewed again, and what minister renewed it.

I ga-ve these renewals a
few moments ago. The renewal from July, 1926, was for two months. Then there was an order in council passed on October 12, 1926, extending the contract from October 1,
1926,	to the end of the fiscal year. Then a new contract was entered into on April 1,
1927,	for three years, and a third contract was entered into on April 1, 1930.

I should like to
ask the minister if he knows whether the exMinister of Customs actually did. protest against the renewal of the contract then.

Is Reuters' service distributed freely on the other side, or is that included in the general service which they distribute, provided one subscribes to it? The newspapers that have the right to the service in Canada have to pay quite an amount for it. It would seem that the agency is in the happy position of being paid to distribute news from this country, and is also paid abroad by those who receive the news- that is, if it is paid abroad. Is the service distributed gratuitously abroad?

Speaking from knowledge of the way in which these matters are handled generally, I should say that those who receive the service subscribe. This is in the nature of a subsidizing of that service, in addition to whatever fees they may secure from their subscribers overseas.

That means, then, that we are paying Reuters to distribute abroad news 'for which the people in other countries are
'
willing to pay anyway. It either means that, or it means that Reuters add to their service something which is not of much use, and for the distribution of which we have to pay them as a sort of advertisement. I do not think, myself, that the arrangement is a very happy one. I am not concerned as to whether my good friend or someone else is responsible. We should never get anywhere if we stopped always to ascertain responsibility in the past. I am interested in the item before us to-day. From what has been urged on both sides of the house I am inclined to support any motion with reference to the matter. I will not offer a motion myself, but if one were submitted I would vote for it.

Before the item is condemned it ought to be examined carefully. I may say candidly that I have given it considerable thought and have examined the material, though perhaps not as completely as one would wish; the time has not permitted that. However, I have looked into it to the point of satisfying myself that the service is a good one, and there is no doubt that Reuters w'ould not furnish the cable service to the extent they do were it not for this subsidy. It is a difference perhaps between a letter service and a cable service, and before taking steps to cancel it I think we ought to be very sure of the grounds upon which we do so. We ought to make sure that we are not doing Canada a disservice- that is, to the trade news of the Dominion, because that is the character of news which the service renders, as a perusal of the journals affected clearly demonstrates.

As a matter of trade news, I do not consider it worth a copper. I am perfectly willing to examine the case upon its merits. Let the minister lay on the table of the house a report of the services given. He says he has clippings. Let us examine the matter on that basis and then judge for ourselves. I have done this already and I know what it is; and, as I said before, I do not think it is worth a plugged nickel.

The point that concerns
me at the moment in the discussion of this item is the responsibility, moral or otherwise, of this government with respect to the contract which has been alluded to here. After all, this government has been in power only eight or nine months, and if it gets abroad that they are beginning to repudiate their liabilities so early in their history, and if that is circulated by the Reuter agency, it may not do us much good. For that reason, if only to maintain the credit of the govern-

Supply-Canada Grain Act
ment I think we ought to allow the item to pass this time. I have a great deal of respect for the opinion of my hon. friend from Lincoln; as a rule he knows what he is talking about when it comes to trade matters. He was in the department, it appears, before the present minister, and when he speaks in the assertive way in which he does this afternoon I am sure he is aware of something which perhaps the house ought not diplomatically to know. I am against the principle-I do not know what my views were when my party was in power-of paying newspapers to circulate news. It at once becomes tainted when the public gets to know about it, and, to use the expressive words of my hon. friend from Lincoln, it is not worth a brass farthing or a plugged farthing-
A plugged nickel.

Plugged nickel, was it? We have in the city of Ottawa representatives of great news-gathering agencies on the other side. We have a reipresentaive from the London Times, a representative from the Manchester Guardian, and representatives from other newspapers overseas. Are we paying those agencies anything for publishing the news they send abroad? I know they are being maintained here as well as or perhaps better than Reuters' representative. Surely if we can pay one agency we should pay the others. Any news published on the other side from the representative of the Manchester Guardian, of the London Times, of the Morning Post, or of any of those newspapers will have as wide a circulation as that disseminated by Reuters agency, and it is free from the suspicion that it is paid for. I am against the .prinicple of paying some people to do work for us while others are doing the same thing for nothing. Either all or none ought to be paid. I trust, therefore, that when the contract expires-and, I was going to remark, when the Minister of Trade and Com-erce now in office has to deal with the matter again, which God forbid-the fact will be taken into consideration that there was determined opposition in the house, not only from the hon. gentleman's predecessor but from others on this side, to the extending of the contract for any further term. After all, $32,000 a year is a tidy sum of money; we do not easily pick it up these days. If we want to borrow money just now we have to pay 5 per cent for it. Surely this is a case where we can take, so to speak,, a newspaper holiday and discontinue this item until better
times come. When the time is opportune we can consider it. In the meantime, however, I am not in favour of cancelling the contract, because we have a moral responsibility in the matter; though on principle I am against it.

Item agreed to.
The Canada Grain Act, including management, operation, maintenance and equipment of elevators, administration of, $2,681,000.
Does the minister anticipate any amendments to the grain act this session?

No, I think not. There
was a very complete revision of the act recently, and what we might call the new act has been in operation only since the close of the last crop year. It is therefore impossible as yet to determine whether the new provisions are going to work successfully or otherwise.
There have been no reports in regard to the operation of the new act?

No. There cannot very
well be any satisfactory reports until the end of the present crop year, which will be July 31.
Have there been any complaints with regard to the operation of the revised act?
No.

I notice a reduction in the item of $203,048. As I remember the revision to the grain aot made during the last session of parliament, it seems to me that the operation of the new act should cost more if that supervision were given which those who sat in that agriculture committee expected would be given under the new act. Referring to the work undertaken by the board looking towards the safeguarding of the producers' interests in the inspection and grading of grain and the changes in the handling and transportation methods, it has become necessary to adjust the methods employed in the inspection department to meet this condition.	'
The chief difficulty found by the new board is in the sampling of grain for inspection purposes. Up to the present this has been done by means of a probe sample taken at inspection. The development of railway transportation. however, i.e., the use of large cars and the heavier weight carried in those cars and the fact that those ears are loaded so fully that as a result it is impossible for a sampler to carry on bis work, requires forty per cent of the shipments now arriving at inspection points to be sampled at unload at the terminal.
There has also always been in the mind of the producer a rather grave suspicion of the manner in which the work of sampling of cars was carried out at the inspection point, and also the definite' proof that the probe sample does not determine the proper dockage in the car sampled in a great many cases in view of the varying nature of this dockage. Also it is possible for a dishonest shipper to so load his ear by what is known as "plugging" as to in some cases evade a proper determination of the contents of that car.
To overcome these and other difficulties the system of sampling at unload by automatic samplers has been devised. A machine has been approved which carries on this work mechanically with niathematical precision and which leaves the operation of the system practically free from human fault, and as a result above suspicion. This matter was very fully discussed with the Hou. James Malcolm, former Minister of Trade and Commerce, also with the Department of Trade and Commerce officials.
fMr. Stevens.]
and with the agricultural committee of the House of Commons. It has also been accepted by the producer at large as being a great protection to his interests. When a clause repeals an existing section, subsection or other minor division of a section, that section, subsection or division, or so much thereof as is essential, shall be printed opposite the clause.

Mr. WILLIAM DUFF (Antigonish-Guys-boroughj: Before the bill gets second reading, it seems to me that as this is a very important matter affecting the public health, we should have some statement from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) with regard to the bill.
