speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: VISIT OF THEIR IMPERIAL HIGHNESSES TO CANADA-MESSAGE OF APPRECIATION FROM THE EMPEROR OF JAPAN
speechtext:
Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that we have recently entertained their Imperial Highnesses the Prince and Princess Takamatsu, I think the chamber would be interested in knowing that His Excellency the Governor General has received from the Japanese minister at Ottawa a cablegram from the Japanese foreign minister, reading:
The Emperor is highly gratified with the hospitality shown to the Prince and Princess Takamatsu by Their Excellencies the Governor General and Lady Bessborough, and with the cordial reception accorded to Their Imperial Highnesses by the government and people of Canada. I am commanded to authorize you to convey to His Excellency His Majesty's personal appreciation.
There is also a despatch from the Japanese minister in this city, expressing on behalf of our recent guests their deep appreciation of the hospitality extended them by the Canadian people.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.
The Canada Grain Act, including management, operation, maintenance and equipment of elevators, administration of, $2,681,000.

Mr. Chairman, when
the committee rose at six o'clock I was asking
permission to place on Hansard without the reading thereof two letters to which I had referred. I find it almost impossible to accept that privilege from the committee because there are, I believe, members on both sides of the 'house who are very much interested in these letters; indeed, I do not believe an intelligent discussion could be carried on without a knowledge of their contents. The first letter, written by Mr. Robert Whiteside, to the former Minister of Trade and Commerce, Sir George Foster, dated at Dunblane, Saskatchewan, January 19, 1920, reads as follows: As your humble servant I desire to seek information which will explain fully the motive our federal government had in undertaking to take over and sell the wheat crop for the year 1919. We fully understand the motive for selling the crop in 1917 and 1918, but one thing we don't know nor have we ever had any report on the same and that was what was the price the government got for the wheat that was exported in the year 191S. We know the growers received $2,262 f.o.b. Fort William but did our government sell it for export on this basis to appear to be good fellows when the price of American wheat was $2.40 to $2.60 or did some one pocket the margins? Wheat and wheat products were the only foodstuffs the government controlled. We feel justified in demanding a report of the wheat that was exported and to get at plain facts regarding the 1919 crop. Every farmer in western Canada is under the impression that our federal government premeditated and entered into an agreement to handle the wheat crop to make gains for themselves at our expense. Note I said federal government; it may have been only members of our government, at any rate it has been reported quite frequently and m bold statements that the time the gram exchange was opened our government did sell or offer for sale some 50 million bushels wheat to Great Britain at a price of $1.75 per bushel and not until the market was open did your government make any attempt to handle the wheat, and we all know the market was advancing and to take control of the wheat when it was at a price of $2.45 and attempt to offer to set a price of $1.75 or even $2.15 does not appear to the farmers as one of good faith, and for the Canadian wheat board to sell to our millers at $2.30 per bushel in the face of prices prevailing on all other products ifoints out quite clearly that our federal government is out to do what it has always done [DOT] and that is give the farmers second place. While I admit we were under military rule and the government had the authority to so act, the manner in which they acted does not show one of good faith, and if the report is really true that our government did sell or offer for sale a certain portion of our wheat any price in the minds of all well thinking men can only come to this conclusion that our government premeditated their action knowing they had power to control things to suit themselves. I further wish to say in all friendliness the farmers of western Canada are determined to demand a report and make an investigation to learn the facts. We intend to outline our plans, decide
Supply-Canada Grain Act

My hon. friend (Mr
Vallance) has opened up a question which really finds its basis in a series of letters which were written by a gentleman named Robert Whiteside from the province of Saskatchewan in the year 1920, and which were answered most painstakingly I think, by the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, Sir George Foster. The letters really might be summarized in this way:
Mr. Whiteside retails to the minister complaints that he hears and suspicions that he
Supply-Canada Grain Act

himself and others entertain to the effect that in the handling of the wheat crop during the years 1917, 1918 and 1919 full value was not returned to the farmers of western Canada. So far as I have been able to see, he does not in his letters support either with evidence or facts his suspicions or the rumours he alleges. In the last letter to which my hon. friend from South Battleford has referred, Mr. Whiteside asks certain questions, and my hon. friend indicated that he did not think that Sir George Foster completely answered them. I think that a little further examination of the latter part of Sir George Foster's letter will clear up that point. If not, I can supplement it with one or two observations.
Let me say at once that I am not at all criticizing the hon. member for South Battle-ford for bringing this matter forward, because I think it is highly desirable that it should be cleared up. Whether or not there are any grounds for the allegations made or suspicions entertained, it is a very disagreeable thing to have such rumours running loose in the country. Mr. Whiteside asks:
What was the price our government sold the wheat crop of 1018 for?
And another question:
Did our federal government or members of our government spII or offer to sell 50,000,000 or 75,000.000 bushels of our wheat crop of 1919?
In regard to the first question I would say that Sir George Foster was not at the time in a position to give the details as to just what price the wheat was sold for. It is quite well known and accepted I think by practically everyone throughout western Canada that the wheat board-
The wheat supervisors?

The board of grain supervisors under Doctor Magill, which consisted of representatives of the producers, the millers, the dealers and the consumers, discharged their functions honestly and well. I think it is generally accepted that this body of citizens discharged a public service and a public duty. If in the present day the house were to demand an audit of the transactions which took place in the years 1917 and 1918 I might as well say they wTould be asking for something which would be very very difficult to carry out. The making of that statement should not in the slightest degree detract from my other statement, namely that the board of grain supervisors at that time discharged its duties to the entire satisfaction of everybody.
Mr. Whiteside's letter implies that members of the government of the day sold

50,000,000 or 75,000,000 bushels of wheat on the grain exchange in Winnipeg and made a profit. That is the suggestion. Well, in answer to that I would say, if I may be allowed to use a rather strong expression, that the statement is absurd. My reason for saying that is that no member of the government handled a single bushel of wheat- not a single bushel-nor did the government as a whole do so. That wheat was handled by the wheat board, a properly organized body. Why was the 'wheat board appointed? The British government had a controlled market; they bought their wheat under government direction an control; there was not an open market. Canadian dealer? could sell wheat to the British government only through some organized body.
Did the British board buy all exports into that country at a fixed price from all sources, the same as they did from Canada, or did they fix the price at all?

I cannot answer that question categorically, but I will give my friend my best recollection. I make my statement subject to correction, because these things happened many years ago and personally I did not have anything to do with them. From time to time the British government would make a bargain or an arrangement for the purchase of wheat from other sources. I refer to Canada, Australia, United States and other wheat producing countries. The prices would be fixed. The wheat board, however, guaranteed to the wheat producer an initial price, adopting a plan similar to that which the pools have since followed. In this instance I think the price was S2.21 per bushel, if I recollect aright. That was the intial price given. Then a participating certificate was given to each person who sold wheat. It is true that a number, small in comparison with the whole, of those receiving participating certificates thought the certificates were worthless and destroyed them. Those who retained the certificates and presented them afterwards received a small dividend.
An hon. MEMBEE: Forty-eight cents.

Yes, a very substantial dividend. I thank my hon. friend for giving the amount, as it had escaped my memory. At any rate through ignorance or carelessness a few people destroyed their certificates and as a result those certificates were never redeemed. The result was that there was left in the hands of the board a sum which amounted to 1467,000. Again I speak subject to correction.

Supply-Canada Grain Act
That was in 1919?
A little over

Probably my hon. friend is right. Out of that sum an expenditure was made subsequently for seed relief, leaving in the treasury to-day, or in the consolidated fund, a sum of about $173,000. These figures I have given from memory. I think however it is obvious to all hon. members that to have attempted a subdivision of this sum amongst all the vendors of wheat would have been a useless task, because the division would have resulted in a unit so small in each case as to make it unnecessary and quite useless. That, I think, is the whole story.
The minister is referring only to the 1919 crop. There has been no reckoning of the 1917-18 crop. We know about the 1919 crop, and we agree with the statement made by the minister in that regard.

The statements in regard to the 1917 and 1918 crop, were presented by the board of grain supervisors. With the exception of this one instance I think they have never been called in question. Even now they are not called in question by allegation backed by any substantial statement or evidence but merely because of suspicion or rumour. I think my hon. friend from Melville (Mr. Motherwell) and other hon. members of the house who come from western Canada and who were active at that time in the matter of handling the grain crop will bear testimony to the efficiency and fairness with which the board of grain supervisors discharged their duty. I confess that while I recall taking a very great interest in the matter myself I do not not remember a single complaint regarding the administration of that board. I make that statement with force because in 1920 on the floor of the house I opposed the continuance of the wheat board. I merely mention that fact to show that I was not an advocate of the system and I gave it a great deal of study at that time. I do not recall any complaint however, and as I say if the complaint made by Mr. Whiteside were fortified with something of a tangible nature which would warrant our reopening the whole question fourteen years afterwards, I would not hesitate to say, reopen it. I submit to the house however that to embark at this time upon an exploration of those activities would be very unwise. The chairman of the board has passed into the great
beyond, and I have no doubt that other members have also passed on. The officers and the staff have disappeared. To make an investigation would be an impossible task.
Surely the facts are on record. There must be a record.

Reports have been made.
I do not know, but I assume that records may be found somewhere. But surely those who have had to do with the question of grain certificates and the innumerable documents involved would shudder at the task of reopening the matter and conducting at this time an audit of that business.
There is money at stake, Mr. Chairman.

What has been brought out to-night, Mr. Chairman, is a most wonderful thing to me, and I do not know anything else that has disturbed the minds of western Canada just as much as this has. There has never been a thought concerning the 1919 crop; we realized that all that was left over on the sale of that crop was returned to the farmers. I want the government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce to keep the 1919 crop absolutely distinct and separate from the 1917 and 1918 crops. The latter are the two crops that we are dealing with right now. You say there was no question in the minds of the farmers of western Canada concerning the handling of the 1917 and 1918 crops. I grant you that, because there was never in the minds of the farmers of western Canada any question but what this wheat was being handed over to the allies in England at a price of $2.21. We thought this was being handled by the board of supervisors, and that it was being handed over by them to the British import purchasing board at that price of $2.21 Fort William. No one thought that there was anything left over. The farmers of western Canada said:	"This
is a patriotic gesture by the western provinces of the part they are talcing in the war". They suffered for it. That was the only commodity on which the price was fixed. While we were being paid S2.21 for our wheat we saw the price in Chicago go up to S3. But to-night we get this letter, and I want to draw the minister's attention to these words:
The wheat was sold during the season of 1917 and 1918 as purchasers were found, and of course for different prices owing to changes in world's market price.
Not for the S2.21; he does not say so; he says that it was sold at the market price. If we take the market price from day to day
Supply-Canada Grain Act

for those two years down in Chicago, which would be ours practically, we find that from
870,000,000 to S100,000,000 was taken out of the pockets of the farmers of western Canada, and we want an accounting.
No, no.

Yes, look it up. Take
the quantity of our wheat sold in those years, and it can be distinctly shown that there was a difference of 870,000,000 to 8100,000,000 between our price and the price that prevailed in Chicago. I think it is only right that we should ask for an accounting.

Why did you not
bring it up in the last nine years?
It was not thought of.
Oh, oh.

I want to tell you
right here that there was not a question of doubt ever raised in the mind of one farmer in western Canada, not one. They all believed that their wheat was sold at $2,21. I leave it to any of my hon. friends here from the west to say whether that is not so.
Hear, hear.

If you had gone into
the west and told them that their wheat had been sold at the market price they would not have believed it. It was not until this year that it was brought to their attention that this was the case. This man received a great deal of credit for having brought it to the attention of the farmers of western Canada. It is a serious thing. I think it is time we got an accounting. There must surely be returns for each of these years.

May I interrupt my hon. friend for one moment? Mr. Whiteside said that he interviewed Sir George Foster in January 1920. He continued:
We-
Using the plural.
-intend on some action at our convention in Saskatoon in February.
That would be February 1921. So the matter must have been fully discussed then.

Excuse me, it never was brought up at any of our conventions until this year. Before this no one paid any attention to it whatever. I leave it to anybody who comes from the west to contradict that. They know very well that absolutely no one thought that this wheat was handed over at the market price. I did not believe it until this year.
You did not believe it for nine years?
Yes, and we were foolish enough to believe the government in power at that time was honest.

Mr. Chairman, probably I can throw some light upon the matter of the sale of our wheat during the years mentioned by hon. gentlemen opposite. In 1917 I went to England with Sir Robert Borden and Sir Douglas Hazen to attend an Imperial conference and to look after other matters. The price of wheat went up to rather a high figure by reason of the fact that a large portion of the 1916 crop was damp.
Off grade.

Yes, off grade. Naturally this portion of the wheat was not very suitable for shipment. Then the matter came up in England about that particular crop. The story is too long to tell now and I will not delay the committee except to say that we considered the crop on the basis of No. 1 northern at $3 a bushel.
Was that f.o.b. Fort William?
Yes.
The 1917 crop?

The 1916 crop. Mr. Lloyd George said it was very fine to have that settled, and the night following the arrangement he made a speech in the Guildhall and told the story of his having bought this large quantity of wheat, something like 100,000,000 bushels, and assured the people that there was plenty of food to carry on the war until next year. Then the question came up before the war cabinet as to what price they would have to pay the year following. They thought that $3 a bushel on the basis of No. 1 northern was a very high price; and so it was. I was asked by the then Prime Minister of Great Britain if I would not fix a price for our next wheat crop. I replied that we in Canada could not do that because the minute we fixed our price, say, at $2, the Americans would put up their price a good deal higher, and this would mean a lot of bootlegging of wheat across the border from the western provinces to the American side and would involve a great deal of trouble and difficulty for everybody. They saw the force of this objection and they said, "Well, will you fix a price for the wheat you grow in Canada?" I answered, of course, that I could undertake to do so only if they would find a way of getting the United States to agree to a price. At the same session of the war cabinet Mr. Balfour was selected to go

Supply-Canada Grain Act
to Washington to see if he could not make the necessary arrangements with the American government. I went the length of assuring him that whatever price the Americans would agree to take for their crop we would also take for ours. Mr, Balfour went to Washington and later came on to Ottawa. On the day following our return to Ottawa Mr. Balfour came to this city, and when he got off the train at the platform here and shook hands with a lot of people who were there to meet him, he came over to me and drew a small sheet of paper from his pocket, which he handed to me to read. That sheet contained the proposal of the United States, which was that they would be ready to sell their wheat at $2.21 per bushel provided Canada would agree to a similar proposal. While I read that Mr. Balfour was standing beside me. I handed the sheet of paper back to him and he said, "Well, what do you think about it?" I answered, "We will agree to that price also," so that price was fixed, and it lasted for two years. At that time I wired Winnipeg asking a number of the grain exchange men to come to Ottawa so that they would understand all the facts. They came down here and we had a meeting in Sir George Foster's office, where we went over the whole case, and they were entirely satisfied.
As for the 1917 and 1918 crops, they were sold on the basis of S2.21 per bushel, and the farmers of western Canada went to any elevator with their wheat, got their money and took it home with them. So there was nothing wrong, and there was no chance of anything being wrong in respect of those two years. Mr. Whiteside is entirely mistaken in his statement with regard to those years.

May I ask a question?
When you summoned the grain trade to Ottawa, did you summon only the grain trade or did you summon producers as well? Did you give any consideration to the producers and ask them whether the proposal was acceptable to them?

No, I did not summon
anyone except those who were handling the grain of western Canada. I have never heard of any individual who was dissatisfied with the arrangements which were made for the sale of the crops of 1916, 1917 and 1918 at $2.21 per bushel. Those who seemed to be dissatisfied were some of the men in western Canada whom you would expect to be the last to have any such feelings.
I was explaining that I asked several people to come down from Winnipeg. I telegraphed the president of the grain exchange to send down six or seven of the best men
to consider these proposals. They wired back that they could come the next day, and they did come. Then some friend of mine in Winnipeg wired me that they should have selected Mr. Crerar and Mr. Wood, who was then down in Winnipeg from Calgary, and someone else, whose name I forget. I immediately wired these men individually and invited them to come to Ottawa, and we postponed any discussion of the matter until their arrival, when we went into the whole matter.
Then there was no supervising body, and this is what happened:	At our meeting in
Sir George Foster's office we were discussing any difficulties which might arise, especially any difficulties as between New York and the grain centres of Canada. Mr. Thomas^ Carruthers, who was then alive, and who was a large grain man, suggested that we should have a committee of certain members of the grain exchange in Winnipeg in case anything went wrong. The idea was that this committee could settle it up quickly, and members of the grain exchange in Winnipeg had the advantage of a direct telephone connection over which they could talk as long as they pleased to New York. If any difficulty did arise, then Mr. Carruthers and Mr. A. P. Stewart, another large grain man in Montreal, would be able to get on the train at night and go to New York and settle up the matter the next morning, so there would be no unfavourable publicity with regard to any mistakes which might occur.

Mr. Crerar
and Mr. Wood both came to Ottawa?

Yes, and then I was asked to name a number of individuals who would see to it that any mistakes which might occur would be attended to immediately. I placed Mr. Wood, Mr. Crerar and someone else on that little committee which was to become active as seon as the grain began to move. When they held their first meeting on September 12, 1917, they called themselves the board of grain supervisors, but they were really a. board designed to prevent any trouble or difficulties from arising, or to settle any difficulties which might arise so there would be no public fuss between the Americans and the Canadians in respect to the carrying out of this contract.
On September 12 these gentlemen met at Winnipeg in order to fix their plans and to determine, how they would be called in if they were required, and so on, but they went further. Mr. Crerar moved that the price of No. 1 Manitoba northern be S2.18 per bushel. This motion was seconded by-
Supply-Canada Grain Act
That is, $2.18 to the farmer?

Yes, S2.18 to the farmer, and that motion was supported by Mr. Wood, president of the United Fanners of Alberta and at that tame president of the Canadian Council of Agriculture. The motion was carried by a majority of the board, though it was strongly opposed by the chairman of the board and Mr. Rath well. Because of this opposition the board reconsidered the motion and fixed the price of wheat at $2.21.

What is my hon. friend
reading from?

I am reading from the memorandum given me by Dr. Magill, who [DOT]was the secretary and president of that board. This is his own document, given me for purposes of reference. So the fixed price, as arranged between the United States, Great Britain and Canada, was the price paid to the farmer for his wheat. England agreed to pay any price Mr. Balfour could get fixed in the United States and Canada, and I agreed that whatever price Mr. Balfour could get the United States to fix would be satisfactory to us. When he came here and it was all settled, he told me he was going home the happiest man who ever crossed the ocean. He said it was a great and successful trip for him, and that his people were entirely satisfied to pay the price of $2.21.
Did the United States stick to the agreement?
Absolutely.
Then all wheat sold by the United States to the British government-[DOT]
Every bushel was sold at
On the basis of No. 1 northern?	o .
Yes.
My hon. friend said a portion of the 1916 crop was confiscated, and that S3 a bushel was paid for it.
No, it was sold at that price.
To whom did you pay the $3 a bushel?
The people got it. Whoever had wheat in this country got every cent of it. They all got it. There was not one sixpence taken out of it in any shape or form.
On Fort William basis?
Fort William basis, No. 1 northern.
The farmers never got $3 a bushel for any wheat.
Remember there was a lot of tough wheat that year-nearly seventy or eighty million bushels of tough wheat.
That would not make it worth more.
No; a lot less. Those are the actual facts. They got more for their wheat that year than they did before or have done since. That is the explanation.

The hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Rogers) has made one valuable contribution to this debate; he has let us know what the price of wheat at Fort William was in 1916. The farmers know what it was in 1919; it was $2.63. Add the two together and your average is S2.S0. Why guess any more about what we got in 1917 and 191S? There is approximately what we got $2.80. But why should we have to guess when there are the records? My hon. friend's memory, I believe, is correct. But why should we take an hon. gentleman's memory as against the records? That is extraordinary. There were three boards successively in 1917, 1918 and 1919 and in each case there was a surplus. It was brought to the attention of the late government that there was about half a million of a surplus in 1919. Two or three deputations waited upon the government and the Minister of Finance at that time, claiming that such surplus was theirs, the farmers': but the late Mr. Robb had to be shown that it was. He would not pay the money until it was absolutely proven that it belonged to the farmers and not to the treasury. He knew that it had been put into the general revenue fund, but he would not pay any of it out to anyone until it was shown, as finally it was, that he was justified in doing so. There was distributed to the farmers some $400,000, leaving in the treasury $100,000 to take care of any possible participation certificates which, having been lost, might eventually turn up. But we are not discussing that at all. I merely wish to show what disposition was made of the surplus that went back to the farmers through their respective provincial governments in 1919. I have shown that. Now what disposition was made of the other two surpluses in 1917 and 1918? That is what my hon. friend from South Battleford wishes to know. The minister says it was a long time ago. But my hon. friend from South

Supply-Canada Grain Act
Winnipeg is able to supply us information from memory. And Sir George Foster said there was a surplus which went into the treasury of Canada; it went into the general revenue fund. Why surround the matter with all this mystery and talk?
There is no mystery.

Well, there seems
to be a desire to becloud the issue:	No one
disputes-

You had nine years to pay
it; why didn't you?

No one disputes
the way it was conducted or the way the business was handled. All the boards were conducted exceedingly well. But we never knew until last fall that there was such a condition of things, and when the farmers came to the former government asking for the surplus of 1919 it was never suggested to the then government that there were surpluses for 1917 and 1918 also. I never knew it; I never heard about it until last fall. I see some hon. gentlemen grinning over there. The audit branch has been increased, but there has not been an increase in the other work of the department.

There is provision here
for S3,720 for an assistant secretary. This is a new position. I should like to know the reasons for .the appointment of this new official.

So much money has been
spent on the Welland canal that it is not surprising that the expenses of the department have increased.

I am informed that one of the officers of the department who previously was rated as a head clerk was promoted to the position of assistant secretary, and that position was created as far as the name was concerned. This meant a slight increase in his salary, but his previous salary was wiped out, so instead of meaning an additional man it meant only a different rating. As I have pointed out, really there has been a decrease in the expenditures of the department of about 83,000.

Was that position created by the Civil Service Commission?
Mr. MANIO-N: Yes.
I see there is also the addition of a principal clerk as compared with last year. Is that a new appointment which was made by the Civil Service Commission, and what was the reason for it?

That is part of the reclassification I have been speaking of. I will again point out to my hon. friend that due to the
various reclassifications, while the staff remains the same the salaries have been decreased by about $3,000, so there has been an improvement instead of the reverse.

I notice that provision is made for a secretary to the executive. We were told a few moments ago that another secretary to the executive is provided for out of contingencies. May I ask if two secretaries are required?
This position was in existence previously. Mr. Pugsley is secretary of the department, and this man is the assistant. This has nothing whatever to do with my personal staff.

The minister made a statement a moment ago which struck me rather forcibly. He said his department audited the capital expenditure of the Canadian National Railways. I think the minister made a mistake. The capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways are voted every year, and there is a firm of auditors, Price, Wlaterhouse and Company, or somebody else, who audit all the accounts of the Canadian, National Railways. Once a capital expenditure has been voted in the form of a loan I do not believe it is audited iby the department. That must be so, since the minister stated that he has nothing whatever to do with the administration of the Canadian National Railways. What has the minister to say in that regard?

I will explain to my hon. friend. In regard to statutory capital expenditure, where the government provides the money, we conduct an audit. Where the railway itself makes expenditures without statute, we do not have an audit. Price, Waterhouse and Company are general auditors for the railway; my hon. friend is correct in that, but with regard to expenditures such as the Montreal terminal, the different branch lines, the Toronto terminal, the Hudson Bay railway and so on, those are all statutory. They are audited by the department, because they go through our department by statute.
I am afraid the minister used the word "statutory" in a wrong way. The minister means money which is provided by a special vote, but that is not what we call statutory with regard to these estimates.

Yes, the money provided by statute. The Montreal terminal was incorporated in a statute, and that was the
Supply-Railways and Canals.

case also with the Toronto terminal, the branch lines and so on. They were all bills passed by the house.
The minister can assure us that the audit branch of the Department of Railways and Canals has nothing to do with the audit of the accounts of the Canadian National Railways?
It has nothing to do with the operating expenditures of the railway.
Will the minister tell me. whether the Auditor General has anything to do with auditing the accounts of the Canadian National railways?
He has not.

In other words, the only audit which is carried on, as far as the Canadian National railways are concerned, is the independent audit by Price, Waterhouse and Company, who report to the Canadian National Railway officials and to no one else. And this parliament, notwithstanding the fact that we are supposed to be shareholders in the Canadian National Railways, has nothing whatever to say in respect of any one of those expenditures made by the system. Aim I correct?

The independent audit of
the books and records of the Canadian National Railways is conducted by Geo. A. Touche and Co., but of course, that is a matter over which I have no control.
I beg the minister's pardon; I should not have asked that question. The only reason I asked it was that he himself had mentioned something about auditing.

My understanding is that the Canadian National Railways have their own official auditors, and in addition to that there is an outside group of auditors who do auditing as well. But where there are statutory expenditures we have an audit branch which audits those expenditures. They audit the expenditures that go through our department, as they also do the canal expenditures.
Expenditures authorized by special act of parliament?
Yes.
On what date was the order in council passed granting $1,500,000 to both the large railway companies in order to provide work for unemployment relief?

There was $1,500,000 taken out of the $20,000,000 fund to provide for the

railways the interest on certain works which they did and which they would not otherwise have done for perhaps a year or two, and in some cases four years. That sum was divided between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National for works which they chose to do-various works scattered around from one end of Canada to the other. These undertakings amounted to something like $22,000,000, and out of that $20,000,000 fund the interest was provided for, amounting to $1,500,000.
At what date was the order in council passed?
I do not think I can tell my hon. friend. It was passed shortly after the brief session of last September. I should imagine it was passed some time in October.
Will the minister be kind enough to give the information to-morrow on the orders of the day?
Yes; I can look it up.
The date of the order in council granting the $1,500,000 to both railways.

As a matter of fact, I do not know that there was an order in council. I am not sure there was. But an arrangement was made with the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific. The Deputy Minister of Railways and myself met with officers of the two railways and we discussed the works they proposed to do, but I doubt whether there was an order in council. There was an agreement with the two railways but I am sorry I cannot inform my hon. friend offhand as to the date. I should imagine, however, it was towards the middle or the end of October.
Can I get the date of that agreement, please.

Yes; I will do the best I
can to get it.

Will the minister give it
to-morrow on the orders of the day?
I will try. '
Thank you.
In these agreements between the railway companies and the government, were the works to be done specified?
Yes, they were.

I have been somewhat interested in listening to the explanations of the minister. There has been

Questions
no change from the custom followed by the late government in dealing with the Canadian National Railways, and it seems to me that my hon. friend is taking upon himself a good deal of responsibility in relation to the works of the Canadian National. My understanding was that after the moneys were appropriated by the government, which moneys were for capital account, the responsibility in regard to stations, maintenance and everything else in connection with the national railways rested entirely with the management and was altogether free from interference on the part of the government.
That is quite right,

I cannot,
therefore, understand why my hon. friend should be responsible for Riviere du Loup or why he should have anything to do with that or any other station.

My hon. friend has misunderstood me. I did not say that we had anything to do with these expenditures except in so far as they are statutory. Riviere du Loup is on a government line, and in the case of government railways the contracts have to come before the government. Such contracts came before the government of which my hon. friend was a member. There has been no change, and I have not implied that there has been any change, with respect to the handling of the affairs of the Canadian National Railways or the auditing of the accounts.
That applies only to government-owned railways that are now operated by the Canadian National Railways?
Yes.
I can understand that. But I was desirous of knowing whether any change had taken place with respect to the Canadian National Railways generally-
Not at all.

-because,
if that were the case, I think my hon. friend would be taking on a considerable responsibility.

I might tell my hon. friend that, by reason of the decreased earnings, the government has taken the attitude that there should be no unnecessary expenditures on capital account. Beyond that, there has been no change.
I understand -that. The government must find the money; but having found it, neither the government nor the minister has any further responsibility.
That is quite right.

I wish to refer for a moment to the definite pledge given the electorate at Woodstock, Ontario, on June 24, 1930, by the present Prime Minister. There was depression in the country at that time, and the right hon. gentleman promised the construction of national highways and the building of branch lines, as reported in the Mail and Empire of June 26.
I may say there are a number of branch lines still being built.

The point is that this was an undertaking to build branch lines to take care of unemployment. Here is an hon. member who wishes to have a station built, a station which is essential to the commerce of the country. I would point out to the Minister of Railways that this work would give relief to the unemployed in that particular town.

Mr. Chairman. I beg to direct your attention to the fact that it is eleven o'clock.
Progress reported.
